name: Aeschylus
credit: Portrait: Tilemachos Efthimiadis — CC BY-SA 2.0 (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Aeschylus (c. 525–456 BC) is the Athenian tragic poet; the epitaph Paton prints under his name is the one traditionally said to have been written for his own tomb. Paton's Index of Authors includes the poet among those of Book VII. The scan of Paton's index of authors used here does not give a date for the poet; the date shown is the conventional one.
This archive carries the 1 epigram ascribed to the poet in the second volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Book VII: 255).

poems.title: Book VII, 255
poems.author: Aeschylus
poems.text: Dark Fate likewise slew these staunch spearmen, defending their country rich in flocks. Living is the fame of the dead, who steadfast to the last lie clothed in the earth of Ossa.

poems.title: Book X, 110
poems.author: Aeschylus
poems.text: A lion cub should not be reared in the city. First and foremost bring up no lion in the city, but if one be reared, submit to his ways.

poems.title: On the Slain in a Battle in Thessaly (Mackail)
poems.author: Aeschylus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: These men also, the steadfast among spears, dark Fate destroyed as they defended their native land rich in sheep; but they being dead their glory is alive, who woefully clad their limbs in the dust of Ossa.

poems.title: On Aeschylus (Mackail)
poems.author: Aeschylus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Aeschylus son of Euphorion the Athenian this monument hides, who died in wheat-bearing Gela; but of his approved valour the Marathonian grove may tell, and the deep-haired Mede who knew it.
